questions.question: Dube Cycles collects credit sales at 25 percent in the month of sale, 55 percent the following month and 15 percent in the second month, with 5 percent bad. Credit sales were July R60 000, August R90 000 and September R110 000. August purchases of R70 000 are paid in September with a 4 percent settlement discount. Calculate September's collections from debtors and the September payment to creditors, and interpret the collection pattern.
questions.expected_answer: September collections, three layers: 25 percent of September's own R110 000 is R27 500; 55 percent of August's R90 000 is R49 500; 15 percent of July's R60 000 is R9 000 — total R86 000. The 5 percent of each month never appears in the schedule: that absence is the bad debts, matching the projected income statement's expense. The creditors' payment is 96 percent of August's R70 000 — R67 200 — with the R2 800 discount earned by prompt payment. Interpretation: only 25 percent of credit sales converts to cash in the month of sale, so the business finances seventy-five percent of every month's credit sales for a month or more, and a weak sales month echoes through two further months of collections. If the pattern worsens, the same sales deliver less cash later, and levers such as credit vetting, settlement discounts and interest on overdue accounts each carry their own cost.

questions.question: Assemble Dube Cycles' September cash budget: cash sales R64 000, collections R86 000, commission income R5 000; payments to creditors R67 200, salaries and wages R41 000, scooter deposit R18 000, loan instalment R8 800, sundry expenses R12 000; opening overdraft R3 000. Then place these items correctly between the cash budget and the projected income statement: depreciation, the new scooter, a loan received, drawings and bad debts.
questions.expected_answer: Receipts: 64 000 plus 86 000 plus 5 000 — R155 000. Payments: 67 200 plus 41 000 plus 18 000 plus 8 800 plus 12 000 — R147 000. Surplus: R8 000; opening balance minus R3 000; closing balance R5 000 favourable — the surplus clears the overdraft, ending its interest cost. The last three lines chain each month to the next. Boundary items: depreciation appears only in the projected income statement, since no cash ever moves for it; the new scooter appears in the cash budget in full in its payment months, while only its depreciation reaches the income statement; a loan received is a cash budget receipt but never income; drawings are a cash budget payment but never an expense; bad debts are an income statement expense, visible in the cash budget only as collections that never arrive. The documents answer different questions — profitability under accrual rules against money in the bank on actual dates — and a business can be profitable and cash-starved, or cash-rich and unprofitable, in the same month.

questions.question: October's comparison: sales budgeted R150 000, actual R126 000; advertising budgeted R6 000, actual R1 500; salaries and wages budgeted R41 000, actual R47 000. Analyse the variances properly and discuss the ethics of budget manipulation.
questions.expected_answer: Label, explain, judge — and read related lines in pairs. Sales are unfavourable by R24 000; advertising is arithmetically favourable by R4 500; but read together they tell one story — the advertising was cut and the sales fell, a false economy that saved four and a half thousand to lose twenty-four. Underspending on causal lines like advertising, maintenance or training must be judged against what the spending was meant to cause. Salaries and wages are overspent by R6 000, but judgement waits for the explanation: overtime for a stock count or a negotiated increase differs from uncontrolled casual hiring — same variance, different action. Ethics: padding expense budgets so underspending later looks like discipline is a lie told in advance that misallocates resources; fantasy sales forecasts shown to a bank corrupt every downstream figure so that money is lent into fiction; and budgets wielded to shift blame, or approved and then quietly overspent on management comforts while training is frozen, publish the business's real priorities. The control cycle answers all of it: budgets prepared before the period, approved, compared monthly with actuals, variances explained in writing, and corrective action recorded — plan, act, compare, correct.
